content: The World Health Organization (WHO) conducted a comprehensive survey to gather expert opinions on school health services (SHS). This survey, detailed in Web Annex G of the WHO guideline on SHS, aimed to evaluate the suitability of various health interventions for inclusion in school health programs. The methodology and findings of the survey are summarized below. The survey was developed in collaboration with global experts and included a master list of 405 potential health service activities for children aged 5–19. This list was refined into 86 potential SHS interventions across 16 health areas, including health promotion, education, screening, immunization, counseling, and care for communicable and noncommunicable diseases. Respondents were asked to categorize these interventions as essential, highly suitable, suitable, or unsuitable for SHS, and to specify whether they should be universally applied or limited to specific geographic areas. Additionally, respondents could suggest up to three additional interventions they deemed essential. The survey was administered online in six WHO languages (Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Spanish, and Russian) and distributed to 1,293 pre-selected experts. These experts were identified through journal database searches, professional networks, and WHO staff recommendations. A total of 442 experts (34%) completed at least the first page of the survey, with 417 (94%) completing all 86 mandatory questions. Respondents represented 81 nationalities, with the most common being from the Philippines, the United States, China, and the United Kingdom. Their ages ranged from 25 to 81 years, with a mean and median age of 51. Quantitative analysis focused on the top 20 interventions ranked as essential everywhere, essential in certain geographic areas only, or unsuitable everywhere. The most highly ranked interventions as essential everywhere were in the areas of health promotion and education. These included promoting personal hygiene and handwashing with soap (80%), providing sexual and reproductive health education (75%), promoting health literacy (73%), educating about nutrition (73%), and promoting oral health care (70%). Clinical interventions ranked as essential everywhere included immunization, screening, assessment, and general care. Interventions deemed essential in certain geographic areas only addressed region-specific conditions influenced by disease prevalence, resources, and climate. The top-ranked interventions in this category included administering region-specific immunizations (49%), promoting insecticide-treated bed nets (48%), and conducting mass drug administration (38%). Conversely, interventions ranked as unsuitable everywhere were primarily related to noncommunicable disease screening, such as hypertension (14%), diabetes (12%), and scoliosis (12%). The survey also collected 378 write-in suggestions for additional essential interventions. These suggestions primarily focused on health promotion, education, and other aspects of health-promoting schools (HPS), as well as assessment, general care, and mental health care. Common suggestions included health education on safe technology use, collaboration with school staff in multidisciplinary health services, support for safe water and sanitation, early screening for developmental and learning needs, occupational therapy, and specific nutrition interventions for malnutrition or obesity. Overall, the survey successfully gathered meaningful data from a diverse group of experts. The findings highlighted the importance of health promotion and education as core components of SHS, alongside clinical interventions such as immunization and screening. The results underscore the critical role of health workers in delivering these services within school settings. The survey's conclusions will inform the development of comprehensive and contextually appropriate school health programs globally.
